title: The Citizenship Test: Clean Up Mohalla
description: Your neighbourhood is falling apart — broken roads, no garbage collection, a corrupt ward officer. Armed with civic knowledge, community spirit, and your phone camera, can you clean up the mohalla and prove that teenagers can change the world?
cover_image_prompt: A 14-year-old Indian girl with a clipboard and phone camera standing in a messy neighbourhood with broken roads and overflowing garbage, determined expression, community members behind her, watercolor illustration, age 10-18 friendly
learning_objectives: Understand civic rights and responsibilities in a democracy
Learn practical tools for community organizing: RTI, petitions, media
Practice building diverse coalitions across age, class, and interest groups
Develop resilience when facing institutional corruption and bureaucratic obstacles
Explore how individual action can spark collective change
learning_concept: Citizenship is not a test you pass once — it is a daily practice of caring about your community and having the courage to improve it.
psychological_framework: Community Organizing (Alinsky) — building power through relationships and shared interests; Civic Agency — the belief and capacity that ordinary people can create meaningful change

scenes.title: The Broken Road
scenes.narrative:
The pothole had been there for three months. It started small — just a crack in the asphalt near the community temple. But monsoon rains turned it into a crater wide enough to swallow a bicycle wheel. Last Tuesday, old Mr. Verma fell into it and broke his wrist.

Zara walked past it every day on her way to school. She walked past the overflowing garbage bin that hadn't been emptied in two weeks. Past the broken streetlight that made the lane dangerous after dark. Past the drainage pipe that spilled sewage onto the road every evening.

{player_name} had always assumed that someone else would fix these things. The municipal corporation. The ward officer. The adults. But nobody was fixing anything. And Mr. Verma's broken wrist was the last straw.

Dev, her best friend, saw her staring at the pothole. 'You have that look,' he said. 'The look that means you are about to do something everyone says is impossible.'

scenes.title: The Ward Office
scenes.narrative:
The ward office was a dingy building with peeling paint and a ceiling fan that creaked ominously. Uncle Ramesh — officially Mr. Ramesh Tiwari, Junior Ward Officer — sat behind a desk covered in files that looked like they hadn't been opened since the last election.

'Ah, you are here about the pothole,' he said before Zara could speak. 'Yes, yes, we know about it. It is in the plan for next quarter. Budget constraints, you understand.'

Next quarter. That was three months away. Zara looked at the 'Citizen Grievance Register' on the counter. It had entries going back two years — the same complaints repeated every few months, each marked 'Under Process.'

{player_name} realized something: the system was not broken. It was working exactly as Uncle Ramesh wanted it to — slowly enough that nothing changed and nobody was held accountable.

choices.consequence_hint: Paper trails create accountability — documented complaints are harder to ignore than verbal ones.

scenes.title: The Decision to Fight
scenes.narrative:
Walking home from the ward office, Zara's mind was racing. The system was designed to exhaust citizens — make them file forms, wait in queues, get lost in bureaucracy, and eventually give up.

But Zara had learned something useful in school: citizens have rights. The Right to Information Act. The right to attend gram sabha meetings. The right to demand accountability from elected representatives.

Dev said: 'So what is the plan?' Zara pulled out her notebook. 'First, we learn the rules. Then we use them. Then we organize the neighbourhood. Then we make enough noise that ignoring us is more trouble than fixing the problems.'

Aunty Fatima, who was watering her plants on the balcony above, overheard. 'Beta, I have been complaining about that garbage for five years. Nobody listens.' Zara looked up: 'Then let us make them listen, Aunty.'

{player_name} went home and started researching. The fight for the mohalla had begun.

scenes.coaching_moment: Every movement starts with one person who refuses to accept that 'nothing can be done' — and then finds the tools to prove otherwise.

choices.consequence_hint: RTI is the most powerful tool a citizen has — it forces transparency on institutions that prefer to operate in the dark.

scenes.title: The RTI Response
scenes.narrative:
The RTI response arrived in fifteen days — as required by law. What it revealed was explosive. The ward had received Rs. 45 lakh for infrastructure maintenance in the last year. Of this, Rs. 38 lakh was marked as 'spent.' But the roads were broken, the lights were off, and the garbage was uncollected.

Where did thirty-eight lakh rupees go? The documents showed payments to contractors for work that was never done — ghost repairs, phantom maintenance, imaginary equipment purchases.

{player_name} held the papers with trembling hands. This was not just negligence. It was corruption. Uncle Ramesh and his network were stealing the neighbourhood's money.

Dev looked at the papers and said: 'This is dangerous, Zara. These people have power. They will not be happy that a fourteen-year-old girl is looking at their books.'

scenes.coaching_moment: When you discover corruption, the question is not just what you know — it is what you are willing to do about it.

scenes.title: Building the Case
scenes.narrative:
Zara and Dev spent three days cross-referencing the RTI data with the reality on the ground. For every 'completed' repair in the documents, they took photos showing the road still broken. For every 'purchased' streetlight, they counted the ones still dark.

Aunty Fatima, who turned out to be a retired school principal with a sharp mind for numbers, helped them create a comparison chart: 'Official Claims vs. Reality.'

The chart was devastating. Of twenty-three claimed repairs, only three showed any evidence of work being done. Almost thirty-five lakh rupees — the neighbourhood's money — had disappeared.

{player_name} now had evidence that could expose a corrupt system. But evidence without allies is just paper. She needed the community behind her before taking this further.

scenes.coaching_moment: Data becomes power only when it is organized, verified, and shared — raw information alone changes nothing.

scenes.title: The Choice of Path
scenes.narrative:
Zara had to decide how to use what she had found. Three paths lay before her:

Path 1: Take the evidence directly to the MLA's office — political pressure from above could force the ward officer out.
Path 2: Build community support first, then present the evidence publicly — democratic pressure from below.
Path 3: Give the evidence to Photographer Priya for a media exposé — public pressure from outside.

Each path had risks. Politicians might bury it. The community might be too afraid. Media might sensationalize it and move on.

{player_name} looked at her comparison chart and asked herself: what approach gives the mohalla the best chance of lasting change — not just one fix, but a permanent improvement?

scenes.coaching_moment: How you use evidence matters as much as the evidence itself — the right channel at the right time creates maximum impact.

scenes.title: The Skeptics
scenes.narrative:
Zara's door-to-door campaign hit immediate resistance. Some neighbours were supportive — Aunty Fatima had already recruited five women from her morning walk group. But others were skeptical.

Mr. Kapoor, the retired engineer: 'Beta, I have seen twenty campaigns like this. They all fizzle out. The politicians promise, nothing changes, everyone goes home.'

Mrs. Fernandes, the teacher: 'I agree things need to change. But I cannot be seen opposing the ward officer. My husband's shop licence renewal is pending.'

Dev's own father: 'Stay out of trouble. These government people can make life difficult for families who speak up.'

{player_name} realized that the biggest obstacle was not corruption — it was the community's learned helplessness. Years of disappointment had taught them that fighting was futile.

scenes.title: The Breakthrough
scenes.narrative:
The breakthrough came from an unexpected source. Zara visited the local tea stall where the auto-rickshaw drivers gathered. She showed them the RTI data — specifically the claim that Rs. 3 lakh had been spent on 'road resurfacing near the auto stand.'

The drivers looked at the pothole-ridden road outside their stand and burst out laughing. 'Three lakh on THIS road? Show us where!' The laughter turned to anger. These were working men who damaged their vehicles on these roads daily.

Within an hour, twelve auto drivers had signed the petition. Their informal network spread the word faster than any WhatsApp group — because everyone rides an auto, and every driver was now talking about the stolen road money.

{player_name} learned something valuable: find the people who feel the problem most acutely, and they become your most passionate advocates.

scenes.title: Growing Numbers
scenes.narrative:
The petition signatures grew: from the initial twelve auto drivers to forty neighbours, then a hundred, then two hundred. Aunty Fatima organized a women's group. Dev recruited school friends. Even Mr. Kapoor, the skeptical retired engineer, signed after reviewing the RTI data with his professional eye.

'The numbers do not lie,' he said. 'Someone is stealing from all of us.'

The WhatsApp group had 150 members. The comparison chart had been photographed and shared hundreds of times. Photographer Priya had been documenting everything with her camera.

{player_name} looked at the growing movement and felt a mix of pride and fear. Pride because the community was waking up. Fear because Uncle Ramesh would soon notice — and powerful people do not like being noticed for the wrong reasons.

scenes.title: Uncle Ramesh's Offer
scenes.narrative:
Uncle Ramesh came to Zara's house. Not to the ward office — to her home. He sat in her living room, drinking the chai her mother nervously served, and smiled the smile of a man who was used to getting his way.

'Beta, I hear you are upset about some civic issues,' he said gently. 'Very admirable. Your parents must be proud of such an active citizen.' He paused. 'I can fast-track the pothole repair. And the streetlight. Done within a week. All you have to do is withdraw the petition and stop sharing those documents.'

It was not a threat. It was worse — it was a bribe disguised as helpfulness. Fix two problems in exchange for covering up thirty-five lakh worth of corruption.

{player_name} felt her mother's anxious eyes on her. This was the moment where most campaigns died — when the power offered a quick fix to silence the noise.

scenes.coaching_moment: When the system offers you a quick fix in exchange for your silence, that is not a solution — it is a purchase price.

scenes.title: The Decision
scenes.narrative:
After Uncle Ramesh left, Zara's mother was upset. 'Just let it go, beta. He offered to fix the problems. Why make enemies?'

Dev, who had been listening from the next room, disagreed: 'He is not fixing problems. He is buying silence. If you stop now, the corruption continues and nothing changes for anyone.'

Aunty Fatima called that evening: 'I heard Ramesh visited you. Remember — he came to YOUR house. That means he is scared. You have the power now, not him.'

{player_name} lay awake that night, weighing the options. Accept the quick fix and avoid conflict. Or reject it and commit to a longer, harder, riskier fight for real change. Her mother's fear was real. Aunty Fatima's analysis was also real. Both were right in different ways.

scenes.title: Taking a Stand
scenes.narrative:
Zara wrote a reply to Uncle Ramesh's offer and posted it on the community WhatsApp group so everyone could see:

'Thank you for your offer to fix the pothole and streetlight. We welcome any repairs — the community deserves them. However, these two repairs do not address the larger question: where did Rs. 35 lakh of our ward budget go? We will continue our campaign for full accountability and transparency. We invite you to a community meeting to discuss the ward budget publicly.'

The message was polite but unmistakable. It was also irreversible — two hundred people had read it within the hour.

Dev grinned. 'You just declared war. Politely.' Aunty Fatima sent a thumbs up emoji. Uncle Ramesh read the message and did not reply.

{player_name} felt her heart racing. There was no going back now.

scenes.title: Priya's Lens
scenes.narrative:
Photographer Priya had been quietly documenting the neighbourhood for weeks. She was twenty-two, a freelance photojournalist with a following on social media, and she saw a story worth telling.

Her photo series — 'Chandpur Mohalla: Where Rs. 35 Lakh Disappeared' — featured side-by-side images: the official expenditure claims next to photos of the actual conditions. A road claimed as 'resurfaced' with a pothole big enough to bath in. A streetlight marked 'installed' that was clearly rusted and non-functional.

She posted the series on her Instagram. Within 24 hours: 5,000 shares. A local news channel picked it up. Then a national outlet.

{player_name} watched the numbers climb on Priya's phone with a mixture of excitement and anxiety. Media attention was powerful — but it also meant Uncle Ramesh and his network could no longer pretend this was a small neighbourhood complaint.

scenes.title: The Interview
scenes.narrative:
A news channel wants to interview Zara. The producer says: 'We need a face for the story. A fourteen-year-old fighting corruption — that is a great angle.'

Zara is nervous. She has never been on camera. Dev helps her prepare talking points. Aunty Fatima coaches her: 'Speak slowly. Say what you know. Do not exaggerate. And always bring it back to the community — this is not about you, it is about everyone.'

But there is a risk. Putting her face on television makes her a target. Uncle Ramesh will know exactly who is behind the campaign. Her family could face pressure.

{player_name} weighs the visibility against the vulnerability. Being the face of the campaign could accelerate change — or it could endanger everything she cares about.

scenes.title: The Broadcast
scenes.narrative:
The interview airs. Zara is articulate, calm, and armed with data. The segment shows the RTI response, the comparison chart, the community petition. It is a damning portrait of institutional neglect and corruption.

The district collector sees it. The state government's anti-corruption cell sees it. And Uncle Ramesh sees it too.

The phone starts ringing. Community members are thrilled. Politicians are nervous. And a threatening message arrives on the family WhatsApp from an unknown number: 'Tell your daughter to stop making trouble. Some things are better left alone.'

{player_name} stares at the threatening message. The fight has escalated. Media attention brought power, but it also brought danger. The question now is whether the community will hold together under pressure.

scenes.title: The Response
scenes.narrative:
Zara calls an emergency meeting of the core group — Aunty Fatima, Dev, Priya, Mr. Kapoor, and the auto drivers' leader. The mood is grim.

Priya says: 'Document every act of intimidation. Licence delays, false fines, building notices — these are not coincidences. They are evidence of retaliation. That is a story in itself.'

Mr. Kapoor adds: 'I have friends in the engineering department. The building notice against Fatima's house is baseless — I can get it challenged in a day.'

scenes.narrative:
A letter arrives from the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights. They are organizing a 'Young Citizens' Forum' and want Zara to speak about community organizing for teenagers.

Aunty Fatima reads the letter and cries. 'Your grandfather would have been so proud,' she says — and then Zara realizes that Aunty Fatima knew her grandfather, which Zara never knew.

'He was the one who built this community hall,' Fatima says. 'Forty years ago. With his own hands and his neighbours' hands. You did not start something new, beta. You continued something that was always here.'

{player_name} holds the letter and looks at the community hall — the same hall where the cleanup was planned, where Uncle Ramesh was confronted, where the cooperative was born. Built by her grandfather. Renewed by her.

She spoke about potholes and corruption, about grandmothers and auto drivers, about a community that decided enough was enough. Within a year, twelve other neighbourhoods had launched their own civic campaigns, using the Chandpur model. Uncle Ramesh was formally charged with misappropriation. The new ward officer became a regular at Aunty Fatima's cooperative meetings. And the pothole — the one that started everything — was permanently fixed, with a small plaque that read: 'Fixed by the citizens of Chandpur Mohalla, 2026.' Zara went on to study public policy, but she always said her real education happened on a dusty road with a phone camera and a stubborn grandmother's blessing.

By the time she was eighteen, the cooperative managed a monthly budget, maintained the neighbourhood infrastructure, and ran a civic education programme for local children. Aunty Fatima became its honorary president. Dev became the first resident to pass the civil services exam, inspired by his front-row seat to democracy in action. And every year on the anniversary of the cleanup, the mohalla held a celebration — not of what they accomplished once, but of what they continued to build every day. The pothole never returned. glossary_terms.definition: Right to Information — an Indian law giving citizens the right to request information from government bodies, a powerful accountability tool.
A local government official responsible for managing civic services in a specific area or ward of a city.
A formal written request signed by many people, asking an authority to take action on an issue.
The ways in which citizens participate in the life of their community — from voting to organizing to volunteering.
The misuse of public power for private gain — when officials steal public money or abuse their authority.
The obligation of officials to explain their actions and accept responsibility for the outcomes.
An organization owned and managed by its members, pooling resources for shared benefit.
Punishment directed at someone for speaking up or challenging authority — a common response to whistleblowing.
An alliance of diverse groups united by a common goal, combining their strengths.
An official examination of accounts and records to verify that money was spent as claimed.
The act of publicly supporting or arguing for a cause, policy, or group of people.
The quality of being open and honest about decisions and finances — essential for trust in governance.
A movement built from ordinary people at the local level, rather than from powerful organizations or leaders.
The responsibilities that citizens have toward their community and government — voting, paying taxes, and holding officials accountable.
The process of gaining the knowledge, confidence, and tools to take control of your own circumstances.
Change that lasts beyond the initial effort — built on institutions, habits, and community ownership.

coaching_moment: Citizenship is not a test you pass once — it is a daily practice of caring about your community and having the courage to improve it.
